always resort to if other measures fail, or are regarded as undesirable, is this: we can poll the whole constituency. Although it may be a little expensive, it would not in some cases be a bad thing to reconsult the people.
Then again the statement has been made that a tremendous amount of labour would be involved under proportional representation in canvassing a large constituency. At first sight that seems to be a great difficulty, and it has been brought up time and time again. I submit, however, that the difficulty is imaginary rather than real. For example, in a single member district with 100 voters the candidate must get at least 51 of those votes to be elected; he must canvass or speak to the electors or in some way secure that percentage of the votes. But if you take a ten-member constituency with 1,000 voters, a candidate in ordeT to be elected needs to poll a minimum of only 92 votes. It can re'adily be seen, therefore, that the difficulty has been grossly exaggerated. I would like to point out also that the practice of going round and shaking hands with every elector and otherwise personally communicating with him is disappearing; electors are voting now for candidates on their records as men who know something about public affairs, and on their integrity; also on the platforms of their parties. I think that the conditions are becoming such that this difficulty will be greatly minimized in the future.
I would point out also that under our present system, the small floating or purchasable vote in every constituency has a tremendously exaggerated influence, and a candidate may feel it necessary or desirable to cater to the desires of this class of voter. That is a most unfortunate and deplorable thing in our public life. I may say, too, that elections <are likely to be cheaper under proportional representation; experience has shown that to be a fact. Where you have joint candidates running as representing any party, as happened in Winnipeg, the labour of canvassing and speaking at the various meetings may be divided between the various speakers. Literature may also be got out jointly. I recall that in the city of Ottawa last December two Progressive candidates-I do not know about the others-got out their campaign literature jointly. That shows the advantage of this system from the point of view of expense of either canvassing or otherwise conducting a campaign. I have some evidence in that respect from Winnipeg, but I prefer at this hour not to submit it.
The last point I wish to deal with is the charge that proportional representation would be difficult, if not impossible, to carry out in large sparsely-populated areas. I am not asking the House to apply proportional representation at this time to our large and sparsely-settled1 constituencies. But I would like to point out that the difficulty existing in a five or six-member constituency in my section of Ontario would be no greater than that which now exists in many constituencies in our newer country in the West-in Alberta or British Columbia. In fact, we can form group constituencies in lower Ontario which are very much smaller, and which can be covered very much more easily by candidates, than was the case in the last election in our north country. I venture to state that there are hon. members here who can give personal testimony to that effect.
Let me also submit to the House that the island of Tasmania, about the size of New Brunswick, is divided into five constituencies, six members being elected from each constituency. They have no particular difficulty there in applying this system. In Australia the senate is elected by proportional representation, each state being polled as a single constituency, and neither have they any particular difficulty there with the system.
Now I turn to Sweden. I quote the leader of the Liberal party in the First Chamber of the Riksdag, who stated in the course of a speech in London:
Although I was in favour of proportional voting, I nevertheless hesitated about the advisability of adopting it in Sweden, In view of the vast extent and sparse population of the country. The experience gained up to now of the method in actual use does not, however, lend support to the misgivings that I cherished. My anxiety lest the then prevalent keen interest in the conduct of public affairs might wane and grow slack has not turned out to be well founded; the various schools of political thought have been represented in right and due proportion, and as a rule by those men whom they severally most favoured. A return to the majority voting cannot be looked upon any longer as a business proposition.
I have in my hand a letter received a short time ago from Mr. Alfred J. Gray, of the British Proportional Representation Society, with reference to elections in Australia under this system. I shall not read the letter, but its testimony is along the same lines.
I submit, therefore, that although there are difficulties in connection with the adop-

Proportional Representation
tion of this system in large areas, we do not need to consider those difficulties because we are not suggesting its adoption over the whole country at the outset. The second part of my resolution, as hon. members have no doubt noticed, calls only for the formation of certain trial constituencies-some cities have already adopted the system, for instance, the city of Winnipeg -and in that way we shall, without committing ourselves to any wholesale endorsa-tion of the principle, start in a careful and cautious way, testing it out as we go along.
In the past this question has been discussed in this House without reference to party. I appeal to the House that it shall continue to be so treated. It is too important to be dealt with as a party question; on the contrary, it should be considered as a great fundamental question affecting the composition of this House- the representatives of the nation who have to decide all national issues. Therefore, I hope that this resolution will receive the unqualified and unanimous endorsation of this House, and that when the next redistribution bill is brought down steps will be taken to put it into effect.

Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members are under a deep debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) for the carefully prepared and exhaustive discourse with which he has favoured the House this afternoon on this very important question. His speech shows deep research, and he has travelled more or less over the known globe in bringing to our attention places where the system which he advocates has been in successful operation.
I would invite the attention of the House to the moderation of the suggestions made by the hon. member. He directs our attention first of all to the fact that last year a committee of this House investigated the question of the alternative vote and proportional representation. I was a member of that committee, and I recall that we heard numerous witnesses and deliberated for some time upon the question. We came to the conclusion, unanimously if I do not forget, that we should adopt the alternative vote in connection with single-seated constituencies in which more than two candidates presented themselves for election; we offered no definite statement as to the wisdom or unwisdom of proportional representation-that is, true proportional representation.
The hon. member for Brant now proposes that we should adopt the findings of
fMn Good.]
the committee in regard to the alternative vote, and that we should make an experiment in regard to proportional representation in two or more great city areas, dividing them up and electing a sufficiently large number of members to give proportional representation a fair trial.
Now, the hon. member resembles to a certain extent that great leader of the Liberal party, Edward Blake, for it was said of him that after treating a question there was very little left to be said by any one else, and that is the condition which I am happy to say I find myself in on this occasion. But there are one or two matters to which I would like to draw the attention of the House.
First of all, just how does this proposed alternative vote work? Let me take the typical case of a constituency in which three candidates present themselves, one, we will say, belonging to the National Liberal and Conservative party-I perhaps made a mistake; I think the name "National" has been dropped, and that it is now merely the Liberal-Conservative party, at any rate, that party which sits next the Speaker on the left-hand side of the Chamber-a representative of that party presents himself; a member of the Liberal party, without prefixes or suffixes, also presents himself; and then the third candidate presenting himself-or herself-will be on behalf of the Progressive party. We will call those three candidates, A, B and C, the names appearing in alphabetical order. Instead of being asked to make the usual cross, the voter will be directed to merely indicate on the ballot paper the order of his or her preference, 1, 2, 3. The votes will be counted, and the first thing those who count them will have to do will be to make three piles of those ballot papers which have the figure 1 put opposite the name of one or other of the three candidates.
Let us follow that operation. On the first count, candidate A has four thousand first choices, and we make a little pile of the four thousand ballots. Candidate B has three thousand first choices, and we make a pile a little smaller. Candidate C has two thousand votes. What is the result? Under the ordinary system A would be elected by a handsome majority, but he would not have had any majority at all. That is to say, out of nine thousand votes he would have had only four thousand. So what is done? C is regarded as being out of the race and his ballot papers are counted and transferred in accordance with the second choices appearing thereon. Suppose C's support-

Proportional Representation
ers were evenly divided in their second choices between A and B, we would transfer one thousand of C's to A, and the other one thousand of C's to B. In this way A would have four thousand on the first count, plus one thousand added to him on the second count, or five thousand. B would have three thousand on the first count plus one thousand given him on the second count, or four thousand. A would therefore be elected by a majority of one thousand. If, on the contrary, it was a constituency in which the representative of the Liberal-Conservative party had by some strange happening got 4,000 on the first vote, and the Progressive, indicated by C, had come third, naturally all the Progressives would have given their second choice to the Liberal, and in that case B would receive the whole 2,000 second choices of the Progressives and would be elected over A, the Liberal-Conservative.
It seems a fine system.

It is a good system because it allows those persons who fundamentally hold the same doctrines, the same beliefs, the same aspirations, and the same desires, to give their first choice to those who may perhaps be personally more attractive to them, and their second choice to those with whom they are in closer union than the representative of the third party. That is the advantage of the alternative vote.
In that event, when C is dropped, the second choices really become the first choices of those voters for the other candidate.

Exactly. It is just like this. Suppose I was a voter in that constituency. I would then have presented to me this problem. There are three candidates. One is a Tory, to use the short word, sometimes objected to but often used, one a Liberal, and the third a Progressive. Now, of course, my desire would be to vote first with the party with which I have been associated for many years, and my second choice would, of course, be for the Progressive candidate, so if the Liberal came at the foot of the poll my vote would not be lost but would go to my second choice, who was, after all, my alternative choice. It is the alternative vote. I say I want the Liberal elected, but in the unfortunate event of the Liberal being at the foot of the poll, I want the Progressive to have my vote. It is perfectly simple, and should work out satisfactorily, as I trust and believe it will.
It was Burke who said that the virtue, the spirit, and the essence of the House of Commons consists in its being the express image of the nation, and we want to get a House of Commons which will accurately reflect every important strain of public opinion in the country. That is practically what Mr. Asquith also said. There should not be, he said, an important strain of public opinion in the country unrepresented in the House of Commons. The alternative vote will help to a certain extent, but proportional representation, I believe, will help even further. We had an election in Montreal last April, if I mistake not, in which two city charters were submitted by referendum to the electors, and I was surprised to find that even some members of the legal profession seemed to regard proportional representation almost as the name of some newly discovered breakfast food. They did not seem to understand it at all.
The mover of this resolution has not attempted to describe to any extent the mechanism of the counting of the voting given under proportional representation. Perhaps he was wise in not attempting before a large committee to describe exactly how the votes were counted, but let me just say this: In order to get the full benefit of the results of proportional representation, you should have a constituency electing at least five members; it should1 be large enough to elect that many. I do not think it needs to be any larger. I am inclined to think that when Winnipeg in the provincial election was created a single constituency elect-ihg ten members, that was going rather far, and perhaps it would have been better to have created two constituencies electing five members each. The work of the voter is simplicity itself. He has only to indi-cote on his ballot paper by the figures 1, 2,
3,	4, and 5, as the case may be, the order of his preferences among the candidates, and the counting of the votes merely consists in giving effect to what is really in the voter's mind. I put the figures 1, 2, 3,
4,	5 down on the ballot paper. What do I intend to convey by that act? I intend to convey first, that if my first choice has got more votes than are necessary to elect him, you are to transfer my vote to my second choice. If my second choice has got more votes on the count than are necessary to elect him, you are to transfer my vote to my third choice, and so on; and inversely, if my first choice on the first count has so few votes that he is hopelessly out of the

Proportional Representation
rate, I want you to transfer my vote to my second choice. If my second choice on the second count is hopelessly out of the race,
I want you to transfer my vote for my second choice to my third choice. The theory is simplicity itself. The actual counting of the ballots requires a certain amount of what the Oxford under-graduate denominated as "that low cunning which enables one to understand figures," but after all, men can be got who understand figures; that matter can be very easily arranged. It may take a little longer to count the votes, but that is a matter of no very great importance. The important thing is that wherever the system has been tried, it has been found to give an accurate representation or reflection of the different strains of public opinion in the constituency.
What are the results of the present system? The present system has had some good results, Mr. Speaker, 'because by reason of it we are found here, but it also has had, in the past, let us say, some bad results. It has often given incorrect verdicts. I think the most strikingly incorrect verdict that came from the people was in the election in Great Britain in 1886. Gladstone was supposed to have suffered an overwhelming defeat when he went before the people with his Home Rule proposals in 1886, but, as a matter of fact, he had a popular majority of over fifty thousand. If that popular majority had been reflected in the representation of the House of Commons of that day, it is quite possible thalt the last half century almost, forty years at least, of strain and struggle and bloodshed in Ireland might have been avoided. That is one of the most striking instances, I believe, of the incorrectness of our present system. Under our present system it does not depend on how many votes you get; it is where you put them. Sir John A. Macdbnald, that great politician, not only in the larger sense but in the lesser sense, understood the situation and arranged the Ontario constituencies so as to hive the Grits; that is, in those districts where the Grits were in the majority he put them all together so that the Liberal-Conservatives could have a greater effect upon the elections with their votes. You might have two cities with precisely the same number of Liberals and Conservatives in each, and you might so arrange the constituencies that one of them would be overwhelmingly Tory and the other overwhelmingly Grit. It is not a question of just how many votes you have got:

it is how you sprinkle the majorities over the constituencies.
I am inclined to believe that in this country, as in Belgium before they had proportional representation, our present system serves to accentuate sectional, religious and racial differences. With all respect the Liberal party may be somewhat over represented according to the votes in this House. But so is the Progressive party, and what is the reason for it? Because they represent, and over-represent and exaggerate, the sectional feeling obtaining in those parts of the country where the greatest majority was obtained. That, I think, is true. Just the same, to some extent, as far as Quebec is concerned, the Liberal party in the House over-represents the Liberal feeling in the province of Quebec. There are Liberals in the West whose voices are not heard and cannot be heard in this House-they are unrepresented. There are Conservatives in Quebec whose voices are not heard and cannot be heard in this House because they are unrepresented. Toronto for years and years, has not elected under the present system a single representative to support the Liberal party, although I do not think I am far wrong when I say that forty per cent of the people who live in that city are very faithful followers of the Liberal party. It is a mistake, from the national standpoint, that the citizens of any section of the country, because of their geographical position, should find themselves cut out from active, efficient and effectual participation in the affairs of the country. These are thoughts which strike me as worthy of emphasis. However, the matter has been so amply dealt with that I hesitate to delay the House longer. What is asked for is the acceptance of a principle which, I think, will recommend itself to every one- the principle of the alternative vote in single-member constituencies, and merely to give a trial to the system of proportional representation in one or two, or more of our large urban areas.

I happen to be deeply interested in this question of proportional representation. Had I been aware that it would actually come up to-day I would have been better prepared than I am. Proportional representation is splendid in theory, but it must be regarded with respect of its practical application to the form of government under which we live. And my contention is that it is not adaptable or suit-

Proportional Representation
able to the British system of responsible government. I see some hon. members smiling; they will perhaps agree with me before I am through. You can use proportional representation in the case of the French and American systems of government where the system is a representative one; but under our system of government -which is essentially a responsible system of government, where the Cabinet is responsible to the House, and the members are responsible to the people, giving thereby an elasticity which is not equalled by any other system of government-proportional representation will accentuate difficulties and will not aid the people in the solution of public problems. As to proportional representation in municipal affairs, I am thoroughly in support of it. In provincial and municipal affairs it may be proper; but in the case of the federal constitution -of this country it certainly is not sound. The idea of the system is to give representation to groups of people. One man may be a prohibitionist, another may live in some section where the racial sentiment is strong; there may be another section of the community where the religious element is emphasized; and another where the people are in favour of public ownership; and so there are different groups of people who, from economic or other motives, or by reason of political affiliations, may be influenced by the idea of differentiating one vote from another. Proportional representation will send into Parliament a certain proportion from each of these groups according to their numbers in the country. But when they get into Parliament how are they going to form a government that will be able to control the majority of the House, and carry out the system of responsible government as it has been developed under the British constitution primarily since the time of Charles I? Suppose we had five different groups in this House. Let me take the instance of France where they have seven or eight different groups, each one basing its political existence upon certain definite ideas with which the others do not agree. Now a matter comes up in the chamber for decision,
Was my hon. friend in the House when I explained what had happened in France during the last fifteen or twenty years with respect to the formation of groups?

Unfortunately, I did not hear the hon. member. But I have had
the advantage of reading Lord Bryce's " Modern Democracies " in which that aspect of the question is very ably dealt with. My hon. friend's position, however, does not interfere with my contention at all, because France has an entirely different form of government from ours. You could defeat the French government in the Cham-bre des Deputes and a new cabinet could be formed there without having to hold a new election. Under the British system, where there is a vote adverse to the government it is bound to appeal to the people.
No.

Well, that is substantially the accepted view although some provinces do not carry out that principle; they are changing the British system but they may be changing it for the worse. Anybody who has taken the trouble of studying- historically our Constitution will realize that it has been built up, step by step, on solid foundations, not on theories but to meet the practical exigencies of the case during the period of some nine hundred years. And so a system has been established which makes the government amenable to the popular demand. Take the United States, and what do we find there? During the course of the great war, President Wilson carried out an unpopular policy but it could not be changed because he was in office for a fixed period of time. His policy was afterwards shown to be absolutely contrary to the prevailing public opinion in the Republic, and he was thrown out of power. But what happened in the meantime? There was confusion in their legislation and confusion in their policies with respect to international policies. The government could not act and be sure of its decision in dealing with foreign powers; it was compelled to wait until the four-year term of the then President had expired. But a change came and there was given to the world the real national policy such as the Republican party has now established.
Now, in this Parliament we might have five or six groups as I was going to argue a moment ago. We will suppose that one group is prohibitionist, another is in favour of government control, a third is indifferent to both these things but is in favour -of paving streets all over the country, or some such policy as that. By political manipulation it is possible for a man to put a resolution on the Order Paper which would test the position of the ministry. But the representative in the cabinet of a

Proportional Representation
group whose interest as a group was affected could not approach the consideration of the question from the standpoint of the public welfare, as a minister could who was sharing responsibility with the rest of the cabinet. In order to save his political existence he must adopt an entirely different policy, knowing that the group that placed him in parliament will take him away if he does not conform to their sectional and narrow view. Now, that is the practical application of the theory of proportional representation.
My hon. friend said he did not hear me discuss the question of groups. I want to ask him whether he heard anything of what I said?

If the hon. gentleman puts it that way, I may tell him that I heard very little of what he said, and if I had heard it, I do not think my view would be changed by the hon. gentleman's argument, having read the words of Lord Bryce and a number of other constitutional authorities for the past fifteen years. I do not speak without having previous information; I come here with some elementary knowledge of this subject, and hon. members in this House are equally well informed, and can deal with this matter on its merits. But there is one point and it is a simple one, namely, that we have a responsible system of government, with a joint responsibility of each member of the Cabinet for the whole. When you divide your House up into groups, and then form a government, what is the result? They will get men from these different groups, just as they do in France. In that country they get the groups together. Strong outstanding personalities are gathered together by a leader, and they form a government. How does this method work? They change governments once a month; they cannot have a strong government. They have a system of representative government, and when there is a division among them, they are not sent back for re-election. But what would be the result in our country? You have a Cabinet of seventeen ministers. Supposing you had eight groups, and each member of a group came here by reason of his allegiance to a particular idea

prohibition or whatever it might be, but his outstanding ability makes it necessary for him to join the Cabinet. Then his responsibility extends beyond his sectional idea, and his responsibility is to the whole country. Suddenly he is confronted with
fMr "Ladner. 1
a resolution perhaps pertaining to the question that affects his group particularly, but the rest of the group decide that such a resolution is not in the best interests of the country, and, upon due consideration, he rather has that idea himself. He is then placed in the position that he must either stand by the joint responsibility of the government or must commit political suicide by going against the group which put him in power. Therefore, when you have the group system you destroy the bulwark of the system of democracy under which we have been operating; that is the principle of responsible government. The majority control the House, and the government is in a position to carry out its policy.
Have we not the group system under present conditions?
We have observed that where group systems are developing, strong governments are going down. They do not act together.
Is there anything at all in the present system that prevents the formation of groups of any indefinite number?

There is nothing to stop any number of groups getting into Parliament and any government being formed on the group system, but what will happen is this: that some wise ingenious fellow will insert, in between the ideas of his groups, a resolution with a direct purpose of testing the strength of character of the ministers, and making a minister say whether he will stand by his country in a broad way, or whether he will preserve his political existence by standing by the particular group with the particular idea on which he was elected.
What is there to prevent the same thing now under present conditions?

I think that now, for the first time since Confederation, we have seen the operation of a group system such as would often occur under proportional representation, and, considering the consequences as we have them to-day, and as we witnessed them in the militia estimates the other day, who would say that that group system is in the public interest?

We have had a very excellent presentation of the merits of proportional representation, and particularly the value of the transf 1 i

Proportional Representation
ferable vote in single member constituencies, from my hon. friend from Brant, (Mr. Good) who evidently has given the question a great deal of study, and I think the House is indebted to him for the information that he has placed before us, even if we fail to agree with him. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) has also, in seconding the motion, given to hon. members a very clear exposition of the manner in which this reform is carried out in actual practice. It is, I think, a fact that legislative reforms, in the history of British parliamentary government, have usually been of slow growth. If we study the development that has taken place in the British form of government-which, after all, Mr. Speaker, is, I think, by general consent recognized throughout the world as perhaps on the whole the best form of government in existence-we find that the changes that have taken place, from time to time, have developed and been brought to fruition as the result usually of much discussion and agitation. It is a testimony to the characteristic of the Anglo-Saxon race in matters of government that they desire to be certain of the value of the changes that are sought to be brought about, before absolute effect is given to those changes. The British form of government, which we have adopted in Canada, rests upon a very definite principle-the right of the people to rule themselves. That principle was established in England, long before it was established in any other part of the world, with the exception of the Netherlands. My recollection is just indefinite enough at the moment, that I cannot give the precise dates upon which responsible representative government, as we have it in Britain and in Canada, came into practice in the Netherlands, but at any rate, as far as the great powers of the world are concerned, this form of government first came into effect in Great Britain. Our experience and practice of it has brought home very clearly this conclusion, that we get the best results from it, when we have the machinery that most exactly expresses the will of the people, and that is absolutely necessary, resting, as it does, on the right of the people to rule themselves. We get, let me repeat, the best results in actual practice when we secure the most complete and exact representation of the people's will in the matter. I know there are those who think differently. In that respect I would include by hon. friend who preceded me (Mr. Ladner), but, nevertheless, to the
students of our form of government the statement that I have just made is a fair and correct statement. My hon. friend from Brome quoted Burke. Burke was one of the greatest statesmen of his day, and he, perhaps, more clearly than anyone else of his time, recognized the soundness of the principle I have just stated. What does proportional representation seek to do? It seeks to advance one step further in carrying out this idea of getting as exact a representation of the people's will in the matter of government as it is possible to do. That is the whole purpose of proportional representation. That is the whole purpose and effect of the application of the alternative system of voting, or, as it is often termed, the transferable vote in single member constituencies. This method, this principle, as applied to democratic forms of government is not a new thing; it has been in effect, it has been tested, in many countries of the world; it is being tested even in Anglo-Saxon countries. As the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) has shown,-and I commend his speech to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), who apparently was not in the House when that vspeech was delivered-proportional representation is not only not incompatible with democracy, but entirely compatible with it, and I maintain that it is essential to the fullest functioning of democracy. It has been adopted by Belgium, Holland, Denmark, Sweden and Switzerland in Europe, to speak only of European countries which have had it in practice for a number of years.

Does my hon. friend not recognize the difference in the forms of constitutions of those countries from that of this country; and does he not think that to adopt proportional representation here involves a change in our constitution so as to make it similar to that of the French where the term of office of the chief executive is for a fixed definite period?

No, I think nothing of the kind, and before I am through, I hope to convince my hon. friend that he is wrong. Proportional representation has been in effect in those countries. It is true their form of governmental machinery may differ slightly from ours; but in those countries their form of government rests upon the principle of the right of the people to rule themselves, and if the machinery in existence to give effect to that differs slightly from ours, that does not affect the

Proportional Representation
principle of the reform which I am discussing. I would draw the attention of the House also to this fact that while those particular countries have had this method in effect for many years, you have less disturbance, and the fullest and freest functioning of democracy as regards the rights of the people in their government.
My hon. friend from Vancouver South asserted quite vehemently that proportional representation is not adapted to the British form of government. I think he will agree with me that the overseas Dominions of the British Commonwealth have, in effect and in practice, the British form of Government which he was discussing, and this principle has been applied in some of those states. It has been applied in municipal elections in Great Britain, and with very great success. Not only that, I find that my hon. friend from Vancouver South is not in very good company when he takes the position that he has taken. I have in my band a leaflet of the Proportional Representation Society of Great Britain, a society formed a number of years ago for the purpose of educating public opinion in that land to the need and the value of this reform. And whose names do I find associated with that society? I find the out-^ standing names in all the political parties in Great Britain. At that time-and this was in 1920-the president was Earl Grey; the vice-presidents were the Right Hon. Lord Balfour of Burleigh, the Right Hon.
G.	M. Barnes, the Right Hon. Lord Birken-head-my hon. friend from Vancouver South would certainly not call Lord Birkenhead a Liberal, at that particular time at any rate-Viscount Burnham, the Right Hon. Lord Robert Cecil, who was one of the pillars of the Tory party in Great Britain; the Right Hon. Sir Donald Maclean; the Right Hon. the Marquis of Lansdowne, who has been an outstanding statesman in Great Britain, and who belongs to the particular political faith to which my hon. friend from Vancouver South 'is apparently glad to give his adherence; the Right Hon. Viscount Milner, another political associate, if I might so term it, of my hon. friend-all down the list, the outstanding men in all political parties in Great Britain have given their adherence and support to the furtherance of this reform.
I might be permitted to quote Mr. Asquith, who, I think, will be generally recognized as an outstanding British statesman. Shortly before he resigned as Prime Minister in Great Britain, speaking on the pro-

posal that this reform should be investigated, Mr. Asquith used these words:
With regard to the Parliament which is going to undertake the work of reconstruction after the war, it is eminently desirable that you should provide an electoral basis which will make that Parliament reflective and representative of the general opinion of the country, and give to its decisions a moral authority which you cannot obtain from what I may call a scratch, improvised, and makeshift electorate. Let us by all means use the time-those of us who are not absolutely absorbed in the conduct of the war-in those months to see if we cannot work out by general agreement some scheme under which, both as regards the electorate and the distribution of electoral power, a Parliament can be created at the end of the war capable and adequate for discharging these tasks, and commanding the confidence of the country.
A Speaker's Conference was formed in Great Britain in the year 1916. I find in that Speaker's Conference the outstanding men of the British House of Commons, men drawn from all political parties. And that conference, in the various suggestions of electoral reform which it brought down to the British House of Commons, recommended precisely the reforms which my hon. friend the member for Brant has submitted to this House this afternoon namely, that proportional representation could with profit be applied, and that, in single member constituencies, the transferable vote could also, with profit and use to the development of the British governmental system be applied in Great Britain.	.
Some hon. members probably imagine ihat this reform has had no application in Canada. It has had; in the province of Manitoba, proportional representation was applied to the city of Winnipeg in the last changes which were made in the election law. In the last provincial election of Manitoba, in 1920, the city of Winnipeg was one large constituency electing ten members. I am not going to detain the House with any statement as to the effect of that change and regard in which it was held by the people of that city. I will quote simply the opinions of the leaders in the Manitoba Legislature upon the result of that principle as applied in Winnipeg in the last provincial election. Mr. Thomas Johnson, who was then Attorney General of Manitoba, made this statement:
I feel that I can truthfully say that I have not now and never have had a single regret for the efforts made by me personally in connection with the introduction of this reform into our election laws. The proportional representation system gives a more truly representative legislation than the system of single-member constituencies. The electors of Winnipeg had no more difficulties than usual, and the

Proportional Representation
counting, notwithstanding the great number of candidates, 41 in all, came off without a hitch of any kind.
Mr. Dixon, leader of the Liberal group in the legislature, also commended the system, and I want, particularly for the information of the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Ladner), to quote the opinion of Mr. W. J. Tupper, one of the Conservative members elected in Winnipeg and a son of the late Sir Charles Tupper. Mr. Tupper uses the following language:
In my opinion the test that proportional representation underwent in this city during the late provincial election was successful.
As I understand the system, It is intended to give representation to all parties in proportion to their numerical strength. The result of the late election showed that the minority parties in the city of Winnipeg received representation in accordance with their voting strength. It, however, did not favour independent candidates, as you will have observed.
I might say that the success of the system seems to me to depend upon the efficiency of those in control of the counting. We were fortunate in this province to have exceptionally able men in charge and the result is no doubt In a great measure due to them.
Mr. J. T. Haig, who was for several years the leader of the Conservative party in the Manitoba legislature, had this to say about it:
I feel in talking to my supporters generally that they are entirely satisfied with the working of the system. . . . Taken as a whole, I believe the members elected truly represent the proportional vote of the community as it was at that time. ... As you know we have had a difficult situation in Winnipeg since the strike last year, and anything that will give all the elements in the community a chance to voice their opinions In Parliament appears to me to be a good thing for the whole community.... If we had had the old system in Winnipeg I doubt if a single Conservative would have been elected, and I have no doubt the Government would have had a larger representation in the House at the expense of the Conservative and Labour parties because they would have had the machinery of distributing the seats, and as Governments usually do, would have distributed them with an eye to the result being to their advantage. Under this system no such thing can happen.
He goes on and makes some further observations, which I do not need to read to the House, commending proportional representation to the people of Manitoba. These, Mr. Speaker, are the opinions of men in Manitoba drawn from the various political parties in that province, and while the persons who give expression to these views differ upon almost everything else under the sun, it is a significant fact that they are in agreement with regard to the merits of proportional representation as applied in the city of Winnipeg.
The resolution proposed by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) seeks rather to draw attention to the matter; he specifically suggests that it be applied to single member constituencies under the alternative vote and that it be tested out in a few urban constituencies in the next election. I think it is a reasonable proposal. The principle underlying it is sound, and I trust that it will have the support of the House and that effect will be given to it at the next general election.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be to the advantage of the House if this resolution could be disposed of this afternoon, and that is my reason for saying just a word or two at the moment.
First of all, may I congratulate the mover of the resolution (Mr. Good) on the exceedingly able speech he has made and the very lucid exposition he has given to the House of this important question?
In a word, Mr. Speaker, I find myself in entire sympathy with the resolution, and, so far as an individual member has voice in the House, would );ke to express myself as supporting it as it stands. In this matter the Government would wish to be governed by the opinion of the House, and if the House approves the resolution the Government will do all in its power to give effect to it as opportunity affords.
Let me say, in regard to the discussion that has taken place and the effect that this resolution, if carried, might have upon responsible government, that I failed to follow altogether the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner). Responsible government is based primarily upon a representative parliament, and any measure that will help to make Parliament more truly representative of the public will must necessarily be furthering responsible government rather than in any way limiting it.

But the cabinet would
not be responsible to Parliament. Surely you would have to change the responsibilities and functions of the cabinet so that an adverse vote would not compel the administration to go to the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend quite sees the significance of the resolution. The government would be formed in precisely the same way under this system as it is at present-out of a body of representatives of the people who could command the confidence of the

Proportional Representation
House. I confess that as I study the question more and more, it is my view that instead of adding to the number of groups in the House, the adoption of what is proposed here might tend to limit the groups. My. hon. friend assumes that every man who runs on a given ticket will be elected on that ticket, hut that is not going to be the effect of this system. You might have any number of persons seeking to represent certain sections of the people in Parliament, but it does not follow that they would all be elected. My view is that instead of a man being returned to Parliament on a minority vote of the constituents, if this system is adopted the only representatives who will find seats in the House will be those who command a majority of the votes cast. It is to ensure representation based upon a majority that the proposal has been made and that this reform is so much needed.
There have been quotations from Burke, and from illustrious political reformers. May I add just one to the number, from Pym, who in the time of Charles I, said:
That form of government is best which doth actuate and dispose every part and member of the state to the common good.
I do not think it is possible to surpass that as a maxim of government; and a system of representation which will give freer and fuller and truer expression to the popular will on the part of all classes in the country is helping to bring about that form of government. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am only too glad to have this opportunity of helping to further an electoral reform of this character.

Mr. Speaker, I admit that many good things have been said this afternoon in favour of proportional representation. I heard all these arguments thirteen years ago in this House when the matter was brought forward by the late member for Jacques Cartier, the Hon. Mr. Monk. We were told then that this system had worked well in Belgium, Denmark, and the Netherlands; that it had been .tried in various European countries, and so on. But the House did not take to the idea, and the suggestion of the member for Jacques Cartier fell on deaf ears. The proposal has remained dormant ever since that time.
There is one point I should like the House not to overlook. Canada is a confederation; this Parliament represents people who entered confederation on the basis of cer-

tain fixed ideas, a certain definite understanding. It was stipulated that the representation of the province of Quebec would be fixed at a certain number and that that was to be the basis for the representation of all the other parts of the Dominion. Now the idea is prevalent in the province of Quebec that the views of other provinces are being imposed upon Quebec without its people being given a chance to express their opinion thereon. In the last election my majority was almost
5,000,	though I left the riding fifteen days before the voting took place. But out of
13,000	voters on the list, 6,000 did not vote. The women abstained from voting, and they did so on advice given from the highest quarters. The stand has been taken by the most prominent members of the church in the province of Quebec that there is grave doubt whether female suffrage is in the interests of the state. The province has refused to allow female suffrage in provincial affairs. Last year the city of Montreal, voting on the choice of a municipal system, declared against proportional representation by an overwhelming majority. I submit very respectfully that notwithstanding all that may be said in favour of proportional representation in the cities -'it has no application in the rural districts -nothing should be done-and I would have to vote against the motion if it was voted on-that would bind this House to the principle of it until the matter had been fully considered and the people of the province of Quebec given an opportunity, through their legislature or otherwise, of accepting it.
We have adopted that method in connection with other important measures which have come before this House, for instance, the Lord's Day Act. This legislation was largely advocated by Ontario and the West. The observance of the Sabbath is viewed in those sections and in the maritime provinces differently from the way in which it is viewed in the province of Quebec. The bill was amended in the Senate-that being the understanding arrived at-so as to provide that it could not be put into effect in the province of Quebec without the assent of the attorney-general of the province. That is, the people of Quebec entered confederation under certain fixed .principles, and they felt they had a right to be consulted in regard to any legislation which affected those principles. I certainly take objection to a change in the franchise law of the province of Quebec through the

Questions
introduction of proportional representation until it has been made an issue in the province and adopted by the legislature.

Is the hon. member aware
that the resolution which I have moved does not call for endorsation of the principle of proportional representation by this House, but only for the creation of one or more multi-member constituencies to demonstrate its working?

There is another point
to which I desire to call the attention of the House. The city of Toronto is often mentioned in this House, and Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier good-humouredly referred to it on one occasion as the city which cheered and honoured him but never gave him a vote. If proportional representation were adopted in Toronto it might work all right, because there and in Winnipeg-the latter city has already adopted the system-the people are largely homogeneous in a political sense. But in the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec we have, broadly speaking, two classes! When the voters' list is made up and taxation for schools is imposed, and so on, we have arrayed on one side the English-speaking people, that is, every one who does not speak French, or, in other words, a combination against French Canadians. I am confident that the French Canadians of Montreal would be a unit against proportional representation. I am afraid that in such a cosmopolitan city as Montreal is getting to be, if we had this system we would see every nationality, wanting representation, and we would have "racial" candidates running, which would not be an improvement on our present system, but rather the reverse. For that reason I am opposed to the principle of proportional representation.

Is it the pleasure of
the House to adopt the motion?
I move the adjournment of the debate.
I have still something to add, and I therefore claim the privilege of moving the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
At six o'clock the House adjourned without question being put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, May 11, 1922
